What's really at issue is the reasonable expectation of privacy. This is all very confusing at this point, namely because of the nature of the infrastructure being used to facilitate the services. Traditionally, the right to privacy has included belongings in your home or in opaque containers on your person. Bear with me for a second here.

When your device is generating continuous geolocation data, where does reasonable expectation of privacy end? I'm serious. These philosophical questions are important, even if they seem pedantic. As soon as you transmit information along someone else's private infrastructure, where does your reasonable expectation of privacy end? Where in your constitution is it explicitly answered? The phone may be treated as your personal property, but are the data that you bounce through the network? Which aspects of those data?

If you are giving permissions to your apps to know your location, in public spaces, where does your right to privacy begin? We aren't talking about explicit communication here, as in monitoring your conversations. It's not simple. The reality is, the company providing you a service knows where the service is going. Where does balancing the fact of that knowledge come together with your right to keep it private? You've agreed to let Google enter your sphere of privacy, but is your anonymous location in public so private that we'd consider it reasonable that it is protected?

I'm not even saying I disagree with you. I favor privacy. But these questions aren't easy. Our laws have not kept pace with our way of life.
